title: LLD interview tips: concurrency, testing and mistakes
scopeHtml: Scope: locks, atomics, concurrent collections, testing, common mistakes and the Java rulebook.

notes.title: Why concurrency shows up in LLD
notes.html:
Most LLD problems (parking lot, booking, rate limiter, inventory) have shared mutable state touched by many threads. Interviewers add "multiple gates", "two users book the same seat" to see if you notice the race.

A race condition means the result depends on timing. The classic: two threads read count = 5, both write 6, one increment lost (check-then-act / read-modify-write is not atomic).

Approach to state in an interview: (1) list the shared mutable data, (2) decide its guard (lock, atomic, concurrent collection, or avoid sharing), (3) keep critical sections tiny, (4) say what you did not make thread-safe.

Worked example. Parking lot with 4 gates, 1 free spot left. Gate 1 and gate 2 both see spot.isFree()==true and both assign it: double-booking. The fix is to make "check and take" one atomic step.

Industry examples. Ticketing (BookMyShow seat locks), flash-sale inventory at Flipkart/Amazon, payment idempotency at Stripe all fight the same double-assign race.

Everyday analogy. Two people reaching for the last seat on a bus at the same moment.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring concurrency until asked.
  • Making everything synchronized "to be safe" (slow and can deadlock).

notes.title: Locks: synchronized and ReentrantLock
notes.html:
A lock lets one thread at a time run a critical section. synchronized is built in and auto-releases; ReentrantLock adds features.

// synchronized: simplest
class Spot {
    private boolean taken;
    synchronized boolean tryTake() { if (taken) return false; taken = true; return true; }
    synchronized void release() { taken = false; }
}

// ReentrantLock: timeout, interruptible, fairness, multiple conditions
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
boolean book() throws InterruptedException {
    if (!lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) return false;   // avoid waiting forever
    try { /* critical section */ return true; }
    finally { lock.unlock(); }                                      // always in finally
}

ReentrantReadWriteLock allows many readers or one writer: good when reads are 10x or more of writes. Kotlin: @Synchronized on a function, or lock.withLock { } from kotlin.concurrent.

Rules: lock the smallest scope; never call unknown (alien) code while holding a lock; keep a global lock order to avoid deadlock (A holds L1 wants L2; B holds L2 wants L1). tryLock with timeout is the practical escape.

Decision gravity. Chosen for correctness and clarity. Alternatives: atomics (lock-free, only for a single variable), concurrent collections, immutability, single-thread executor. Breaks when the lock is too coarse (throughput collapse; one global lock serializes all gates) or ordered wrongly (deadlock). Reversible if the locking is hidden behind the class API.

Common interview traps.

  • unlock() not in finally: an exception leaves the lock held forever.
  • Locking on a public object or a String literal.
  • Nested locks in different orders.

notes.title: Atomics and CAS
notes.html:
Atomic classes update a single variable without a lock, using compare-and-swap (CAS): "set to new only if it is still the old value".

AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
counter.incrementAndGet();                         // thread-safe ++

// check-then-act made atomic
AtomicBoolean taken = new AtomicBoolean(false);
if (taken.compareAndSet(false, true)) { /* only one thread wins */ }

// retry loop for a custom update
int prev, next;
do { prev = value.get(); next = Math.min(prev + 1, MAX); }
while (!value.compareAndSet(prev, next));

Related: LongAdder (much faster than AtomicLong under heavy contention for counters, because it spreads updates over cells), AtomicReference<T> for swapping an immutable snapshot, AtomicReferenceFieldUpdater (rare).

Limits: atomics protect ONE variable. Two related fields (balance and version) need a lock or one AtomicReference to an immutable holder. Under heavy contention CAS retries burn CPU.

Kotlin: java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger works as is; kotlinx.atomicfu is a multiplatform option.

Worked example. A rate limiter counting requests: AtomicInteger for a per-second counter is fine at about 100k ops/s; at millions per second prefer LongAdder. Counting AND resetting the window together needs a lock or a single AtomicReference<Window>.

Industry examples. ConcurrentHashMap uses CAS for bin insertion; Netty and Disruptor use CAS-based queues; Android AtomicBoolean for single-shot callbacks.

Everyday analogy. Editing a shared doc: you save only if nobody changed it since you opened it; otherwise reload and retry.

Common interview traps.

  • Using two atomics and assuming the pair is atomic.
  • ABA problem (value changes A to B to A; CAS thinks nothing changed). Mention AtomicStampedReference if asked.

notes.title: Thread-safe collections and executors
notes.html:
Do not hand-roll thread safety if the JDK has it.

Need Use Note
Shared map ConcurrentHashMap use compute, computeIfAbsent, merge for atomic updates
Producer-consumer BlockingQueue (ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue) built-in back-pressure
Read-mostly list CopyOnWriteArrayList writes copy the array; fine for listeners
Sorted concurrent ConcurrentSkipListMap
Wrap a plain collection Collections.synchronizedList compound ops still need external lock
Run tasks ExecutorService bounded pool, never raw new Thread per request 
// WRONG: check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap is NOT atomic
if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v);
// RIGHT
map.putIfAbsent(k, v);
map.computeIfAbsent(k, key -> new Counter());
map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);

Executors: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) uses an unbounded queue (can blow memory); production code builds ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and a rejection policy. Sizing rule of thumb: CPU-bound = cores, I/O-bound = cores x (1 + wait/compute). Java 21 adds virtual threads (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) for I/O-bound workloads.

Kotlin: coroutines with Mutex (suspending lock) and Dispatchers.Default/IO; ConcurrentHashMap is still used.

Decision gravity. Prefer these over locks because they are tested and correct. Breaks when you assume compound operations are atomic. Reversible.

Industry examples. Tomcat/Jetty request thread pools, Kafka consumer threads, Hystrix/resilience4j bulkheads (bounded pools per dependency).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating ConcurrentHashMap as making your whole method thread-safe.
  • Executors.newFixedThreadPool with an unbounded queue in a "production" answer.
  • Iterating a synchronizedList without holding its lock.

notes.title: Putting it together: a booking example
notes.html:
The single most common pattern: protect "check and take" atomically, and keep it per resource, not global.

// BEFORE: race, two gates can both book the spot
Spot s = level.findFree(type);
if (s != null) { s.setTaken(true); return new Ticket(s); }

// AFTER: atomic claim per spot, no global lock
class Spot {
    private final AtomicBoolean taken = new AtomicBoolean(false);
    boolean tryClaim() { return taken.compareAndSet(false, true); }
    void release()     { taken.set(false); }
}
Optional<Ticket> park(VehicleType type) {
    for (Spot s : level.candidates(type)) {
        if (s.tryClaim()) return Optional.of(new Ticket(s));   // only one thread wins a given spot
    }
    return Optional.empty();   // full
}

Kotlin variant of the claim: val taken = AtomicBoolean(false); fun tryClaim() = taken.compareAndSet(false, true).

Alternative: one lock per level (ReentrantLock inside Level) so gates on different levels do not block each other. Global lock is simplest but a bottleneck at scale; CAS per spot has the highest throughput.

Idempotency and release: unpark should be safe to call twice (second call returns "already released"); remove the ticket from a ConcurrentHashMap with remove(id) which returns the old value atomically, so only one caller wins.

Worked example. 4 gates x 200 cars/s each = 800 claims/s; per-spot CAS handles that in microseconds; a global lock would still be fine at this scale but would serialize everything and is the first thing to mention as a trade-off.

Industry examples. Seat booking uses a short TTL hold (like a 10-minute lock in Redis) before payment; the DB version is UPDATE seats SET status='HELD' WHERE id=? AND status='FREE' and checking rows affected = 1, the same CAS idea.

Everyday analogy. Hanging your coat on a hook: if the hook is already taken your attempt simply fails and you try the next.

Common interview traps.

  • One global synchronized method for everything.
  • Returning a ticket before the claim succeeds.
  • No answer for "what if the process crashes?" (LLD is in-memory; say persistence would be a repository with transactions).

notes.title: Testing an LLD solution
notes.html:
Show you can test: a few fast unit tests that cover the happy path, edges and a concurrency check. Tests also prove your design is injectable.

What to test:

  • Happy path: park then unpark returns the right fee.
  • Edges: full lot, invalid ticket, double unpark, zero duration, null input.
  • Rules: pricing boundaries (59 min vs 61 min, rounding).
  • Concurrency: many threads claiming a limited resource; assert no oversell.
@Test void neverOversellsSpots() throws Exception {
    Level level = new Level(10);                       // 10 spots
    ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
    AtomicInteger success = new AtomicInteger();
    CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1), done = new CountDownLatch(100);
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) pool.submit(() -> {
        try { go.await(); if (level.park(CAR).isPresent()) success.incrementAndGet(); }
        catch (InterruptedException ignored) {}
        finally { done.countDown(); }
    });
    go.countDown(); done.await();
    assertEquals(10, success.get());                   // exactly 10, never 11
    pool.shutdown();
}

Injectable time is a design point: pass a Clock (java.time) so fee tests do not sleep: new ParkingLot(pricing, Clock.fixed(...)).

Kotlin variant: use JUnit 5 or Kotest; runTest and virtual time for coroutine code.

A concurrency test can pass by luck; run it many times and treat a flaky failure as a real bug. Tools for deeper checking: jcstress, ThreadSanitizer-like detectors for native, and code review of lock order.

Industry examples. JUnit 5 and Mockito are standard; Netflix and Google tests use fake clocks and fakes over mocks where possible.

Everyday analogy. A seatbelt check before driving: cheap and catches the disaster.

Common interview traps.

  • Sleeping in tests (Thread.sleep) instead of latches or fake clocks.
  • Mocking everything so the test proves nothing.
  • Declaring "thread-safe" without a test or reasoning.

notes.title: Common mistakes: god class and premature patterns
notes.html:
Mistake 1: the god class. One class (ParkingLot, Manager, System) holds data, rules, pricing, persistence and printing. It is hard to test, to change, to lock.

// BEFORE
class ParkingLot {
    List<Spot> spots; Map<String,Ticket> tickets;
    Ticket park(...) {...}  Money price(...) {...}  void saveToFile() {...}  void sendSms() {...}
}
// AFTER: one reason to change each
class ParkingLot { /* orchestrates */ }
class SpotAllocator { /* choose a spot */ }
class PricingStrategy { /* fee */ }
interface TicketRepository { /* save/find */ }
interface Notifier { /* send */ }

Mistake 2: premature patterns. Strategy, Factory, Observer and Singleton added with one implementation and no varying requirement. It looks impressive and reads as over-engineering. Use a pattern when you can name the second variant it enables.

Other classic mistakes:

  • Primitive obsession: String for ids and double for money. Use value types (TicketId) and BigDecimal or integer paise.
  • Public mutable fields and anemic data bags with all logic in a manager.
  • Inheritance for reuse instead of composition (Car extends Vehicle fine, ParkingLot extends ArrayList not).
  • Singleton or static state everywhere (kills tests and concurrency).
  • Not handling failure: returning null instead of Optional or a clear exception.
  • Catching Exception and swallowing it.

Decision gravity. Splitting is cheap early and expensive after 2,000 lines. Add a pattern only after a second concrete need; refactoring to a pattern later is usually easy because of small classes.

Worked example. A 600-line Manager with 25 methods takes 40 minutes to reason about; five 100-line classes each have a one-sentence purpose and can be locked and tested independently.

Industry examples. Fowler's "Refactoring" calls this Large Class / Divergent Change; code-review tools (SonarQube) flag classes over a complexity threshold.

Everyday analogy. One employee being cashier, chef, cleaner and accountant at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Defending a 300-line class as "simple".
  • Naming 6 patterns and applying none correctly.
  • double for money in front of a fintech interviewer.

notes.title: The Java rulebook for LLD answers
notes.html:
A short checklist of habits that make Java LLD code look senior.

  1. Immutability by default: final fields, record (Java 16+) for value objects, List.copyOf in constructors.
  2. Program to interfaces, inject dependencies via constructor.
  3. Fail fast: Objects.requireNonNull, IllegalArgumentException for bad input, IllegalStateException for bad state. No null returns for "not found": use Optional.
  4. Money: BigDecimal or integer minor units (paise/cents), never double.
  5. Time: java.time (Instant, Duration), inject Clock.
  6. equals/hashCode together for keys in maps; records give them free.
  7. Enums for closed sets (can hold behavior); sealed interface (Java 17) for closed hierarchies.
  8. Encapsulation: private fields, tell-do-not-ask, return unmodifiable views.
  9. Small methods (a screen), early returns, no deep nesting.
  10. Concurrency: document thread-safety ("immutable", "guarded by lock", "not thread-safe"); lock in try/finally; prefer concurrent collections.
  11. Checked vs unchecked: domain errors as small unchecked exceptions; never swallow InterruptedException (restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt()).
  12. No static mutable state. Not Singleton for business objects.
  13. Streams for transforms, loops for clarity when side effects exist.
  14. Names over comments: comment the why only.
public record Ticket(String id, int spotId, Instant entry) {
    public Ticket {                       // compact constructor validates
        Objects.requireNonNull(id); Objects.requireNonNull(entry);
        if (spotId < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("spotId");
    }
}

Kotlin equivalents: data class with require(...), val over var, nullable types instead of Optional, sealed interface, when exhaustiveness, extension functions sparingly.

Worked example. Replacing double fee with long feePaise and Duration input avoids a rounding bug (0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3); the interviewer notices in one line.

Industry examples. Effective Java (Bloch), Google Java Style Guide, Spring's use of constructor injection, Kotlin coding conventions on val and null-safety.

Everyday analogy. A pilot's checklist: boring, and it prevents the accident.

Common interview traps.

  • Mutable DTOs shared across threads.
  • Catching InterruptedException and ignoring it.
  • Using Date/Calendar or SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Concurrency in LLD: list shared mutable state, guard it, keep critical sections small; fix "check-then-act" races with atomic claim operations.
  • Tools in order of preference: immutability, concurrent collections (computeIfAbsent, merge), atomics/CAS for one variable, locks (ReentrantLock with tryLock, always finally unlock) for multi-field invariants, bounded executors.
  • Avoid deadlock with a global lock order or timeouts; avoid a single global lock when per-resource guarding is easy.
  • Test: happy path, edges, pricing boundaries, a multi-thread no-oversell test; inject Clock; no sleeps.
  • Common mistakes: god class, premature patterns, primitive obsession, double money, null returns, static state.
  • Java rulebook: immutable, interface plus constructor injection, fail fast, Optional, BigDecimal/minor units, java.time, records and sealed types, documented thread-safety.

questions.promptHtml: Why does concurrency come up in nearly every LLD problem, and how do you approach shared state in an interview?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Multiple gates" or "two users book the same seat" tests whether you notice check-then-act races without being prompted.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Most LLD systems (parking lot, booking, rate limiter, inventory) have shared mutable state touched by many threads. A race condition means the result depends on timing, such as two threads reading count = 5 and both writing 6, losing an update. My approach: list the shared mutable data, choose a guard for each (lock, atomic, concurrent collection, or avoid sharing), keep critical sections tiny, and say what I did not make thread-safe.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Parking lot with 4 gates and one free spot: gates 1 and 2 both see spot.isFree()==true and both assign it. The fix is to make "check and take" one atomic step.

Thread A: read 5 -> write 6
Thread B: read 5 -> write 6     (one increment lost)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring concurrency until asked.
  • Making everything synchronized "to be safe": slow and deadlock-prone.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is check-then-act? -> A condition checked then acted on non-atomically, so the condition may be stale.
  2. Where does shared state hide? -> Counters, maps, availability flags, caches.
  3. What do you leave unsafe? -> Say it: "single-threaded demo code; the repository is not synchronized".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: adds synchronized everywhere. Senior: identifies the invariant, per-resource guarding, and tests it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Flash-sale inventory and seat booking fight the same double-assign race.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use synchronized and when ReentrantLock? What rules keep locking safe?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks practical locking: timeouts, finally, lock scope and ordering.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: synchronized is the simplest and auto-releases. I choose ReentrantLock when I need tryLock with a timeout, interruptible waits, fairness or several conditions. Rules: lock the smallest scope, always unlock() in finally, never call alien code while holding a lock, and use a global lock order or timeouts to avoid deadlock.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: ReentrantReadWriteLock fits when reads are 10x writes or more. A lock too coarse (one global lock) serializes all gates; locks in different orders produce deadlock (A holds L1 wants L2; B holds L2 wants L1).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
boolean book() throws InterruptedException {
    if (!lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) return false;
    try { /* critical section */ return true; }
    finally { lock.unlock(); }
}
private val lock = ReentrantLock()
fun book(): Boolean {
    if (!lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) return false
    try { return true } finally { lock.unlock() }
}
// or: lock.withLock { ... }  or  @Synchronized fun

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• unlock() not in finally.
  • Locking on a public object or a String literal.
  • Nested locks in different orders.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is synchronized reentrant? -> Yes; the same thread can re-enter.
  2. How do you avoid deadlock? -> Global ordering, tryLock with timeout, or avoid nested locks.
  3. When is a read-write lock worth it? -> Read-heavy (10x or more) with non-trivial read time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "synchronized is slower". Senior: scope, ordering, timeouts, and hiding locks behind the class API.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A request thread holding a lock while calling an external API stalled every other request for 30 seconds.

questions.contextHtml:
A word-count service uses a ConcurrentHashMap and still produces wrong counts under load (expected 100,000, observed 96,000-99,000 varying per run). The author says "it is a concurrent map, so it is thread-safe".

Map<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
void add(String w) {
    if (!counts.containsKey(w)) counts.put(w, 0);
    counts.put(w, counts.get(w) + 1);
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Wraps add in synchronized without saying why the map is not enough, or switches to Hashtable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is add called from many threads? Are counts only incremented? Do we need the counts consistent across keys?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the method, then rerun the load test.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) get-then-put is a read-modify-write, not atomic; (b) containsKey/put check-then-act race; (c) the map implementation itself (red herring: it is correct per operation).
  4. How I'd verify each: 16 threads x 6,250 increments of one key: the final count is below 100,000.
  5. Root cause: Each map operation is atomic, but the sequence is not.
  6. Fix: Use the atomic compound operation.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
counts.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);
// or: counts.computeIfAbsent(w, k -> new LongAdder()).increment();
counts.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum)
  1. Prevention: Test with many threads and exact total; review rule: no containsKey followed by put.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use Collections.synchronizedMap (compound ops still need an external lock) or make the whole method synchronized (serializes unrelated keys).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Very hot single key? -> LongAdder values to reduce CAS contention.
  • Is merge's function allowed to be slow? -> No; keep it short, it may hold a bin lock.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite metrics service undercounted by 3% for months because of exactly this sequence.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "map is thread-safe".
  • Hire: merge/compute with the read-modify-write explanation.
  • Strong hire: also covers LongAdder, short lambda rule and the test.

questions.contextHtml:
A seat-booking class for a theatre with 200 seats. During a launch with 3,000 concurrent users, 14 seats were sold twice. The code:

Seat s = show.findFree(category);
if (s != null) { s.setTaken(true); return new Ticket(s); }
return null;

The author wants one global synchronized method. The booking API averages 400 requests/s at peak; each booking takes about 1 ms of CPU.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the race, fix it, and say whether a global lock is acceptable.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a global lock and says it is done, without the throughput or hold-time reasoning.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single process or multiple pods (a JVM lock does not protect across pods)? Is there a payment step holding the seat? Hold TTL?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a global lock as a stopgap and reconcile duplicates.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) check-then-act on taken; (b) findFree returns the same seat to two threads; (c) payment flow reassigns (red herring, duplicates appear before payment).
  4. How I'd verify each: Stress test: 100 threads, 10 seats: success count exceeds 10.
  5. Root cause: findFree plus setTaken is not atomic.
  6. Fix: Atomic claim per seat; return an Optional.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Seat {
    private final AtomicBoolean taken = new AtomicBoolean(false);
    boolean tryClaim() { return taken.compareAndSet(false, true); }
    void release()     { taken.set(false); }
}
Optional<Ticket> book(Category c) {
    for (Seat s : show.candidates(c)) if (s.tryClaim()) return Optional.of(new Ticket(s));
    return Optional.empty();
}
class Seat { private val taken = AtomicBoolean(false); fun tryClaim() = taken.compareAndSet(false, true) }
fun book(c: Category): Ticket? = show.candidates(c).firstOrNull { it.tryClaim() }?.let { Ticket(it) }

At 400 requests/s x 1 ms = 40% busy, a global lock works but queues under bursts; per-seat CAS has the highest throughput. For multiple pods, the DB equivalent is UPDATE seats SET status='HELD' WHERE id=? AND status='FREE' and checking rows affected equals 1. 7. Prevention: A concurrency test asserting no oversell; idempotent release. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not return the ticket before the claim succeeds, and I would not rely on a JVM lock in a multi-pod deployment.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Seat held during payment? -> TTL hold with expiry; release on timeout.
  • Process crashes? -> In-memory state is lost; persistence needs a repository and transactions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite sale oversold 14 seats; the fix was the conditional update, not more locks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lock only.
  • Hire: atomic claim per resource.
  • Strong hire: global vs per-seat trade-off, multi-pod DB equivalent, TTL hold.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service transfers money between accounts. Under load the thread dump shows two threads blocked forever:

"T1" waiting to lock <0x7f1> (Account B), holding <0x7e0> (Account A)
"T2" waiting to lock <0x7e0> (Account A), holding <0x7f1> (Account B)
Found one Java-level deadlock.
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    synchronized (from) { synchronized (to) { from.debit(amt); to.credit(amt); } }
}

Both transfer(A,B) and transfer(B,A) run concurrently.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the service" or "use a single global lock" without the trade-off.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can an account transfer to itself? Do accounts have a unique id? Is a DB transaction involved?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart stuck pods; the dump identifies the cycle.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lock-order inversion; (b) nested locks plus alien code; (c) thread starvation (red herring: threads are BLOCKED on monitors).
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack <pid> shows "Found one Java-level deadlock".
  5. Root cause: Locks acquired in argument order, so opposite transfers take them in opposite order.
  6. Fix: Global lock order by id.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
void transfer(Account a, Account b, long amt) {
    Account first = a.id() < b.id() ? a : b, second = first == a ? b : a;
    synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { a.debit(amt); b.credit(amt); } }
}
fun transfer(a: Account, b: Account, amt: Long) {
    val (first, second) = if (a.id < b.id) a to b else b to a
    synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { a.debit(amt); b.credit(amt) } }
}

For equal ids (self-transfer) reject early. Alternative: tryLock with timeout and retry. 7. Prevention: Document lock order; a test running A->B and B->A in a loop. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A single global lock removes deadlock but serializes all transfers; I would not use it at scale.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ids equal in a hash collision? -> Use a unique id, not hashCode.
  • Distributed across services? -> DB row locks in id order or a saga; JVM locks do not apply.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite fintech outage: two opposing batch transfers deadlocked at month end.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart.
  • Hire: ordering by id.
  • Strong hire: explains the thread dump, tryLock alternative, self-transfer and distributed note.

questions.promptHtml: How does compare-and-swap work, when do you choose atomics over locks, and what are their limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Atomics are the preferred answer for single-variable races; the limits show depth.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CAS sets a variable to a new value only if it still holds the expected old value, as one atomic hardware step. Atomics (AtomicInteger, AtomicBoolean, AtomicReference) protect one variable lock-free, great for counters and "claim" flags. Limits: they cover one variable only, so two related fields need a lock or one AtomicReference to an immutable holder; heavy contention burns CPU in retries; and the ABA problem exists.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: For counters under heavy contention LongAdder spreads updates over cells and beats AtomicLong.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
AtomicBoolean taken = new AtomicBoolean(false);
if (taken.compareAndSet(false, true)) { /* only one thread wins */ }
int prev, next;
do { prev = value.get(); next = Math.min(prev + 1, MAX); } while (!value.compareAndSet(prev, next));
val taken = AtomicBoolean(false)
if (taken.compareAndSet(false, true)) { /* winner */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Two atomics assumed atomic as a pair.
  • Ignoring ABA (value A to B to A); AtomicStampedReference addresses it.
  • Using atomics for a multi-field invariant.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When LongAdder? -> Many writers, read rarely (metrics).
  2. How to update two fields atomically? -> A lock, or one AtomicReference to an immutable snapshot.
  3. Is CAS always faster than a lock? -> Not under heavy contention; retries burn CPU.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "atomics are lock-free". Senior: single-variable scope, contention behaviour, ABA.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Rate-limiter counters at about 100k ops/s are fine on AtomicInteger; at millions per second LongAdder is needed.

questions.contextHtml:
A rate limiter allows 100 requests per second per user. A load test with 16 threads shows up to 140 requests per second admitted at window boundaries. The code:

AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();
AtomicLong windowStart = new AtomicLong(System.currentTimeMillis());
boolean allow() {
    long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
    if (now - windowStart.get() >= 1000) { windowStart.set(now); count.set(0); }
    return count.incrementAndGet() <= 100;
}
questions.promptHtml: Why is it wrong despite using atomics, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Atomics are thread-safe, so the algorithm must be wrong" without locating the pair race.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Fixed or sliding window? Per user (many instances)? Is a small overshoot acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a lock around allow for correctness at this scale.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) window reset is two separate atomic writes with an increment interleaving between them; (b) two threads both reset and zero out each other's counts; (c) clock jump (red herring: currentTimeMillis can step, but not the cause here).
  4. How I'd verify each: Interleave test around the boundary; log count after resets.
  5. Root cause: windowStart and count form one invariant, but atomics protect one variable each.
  6. Fix: One immutable window state in an AtomicReference, updated with CAS, or a lock.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
record Window(long start, int count) {}
AtomicReference<Window> ref = new AtomicReference<>(new Window(now(), 0));
boolean allow() {
    long now = System.nanoTime() / 1_000_000;
    while (true) {
        Window w = ref.get();
        Window n = now - w.start() >= 1000 ? new Window(now, 1) : new Window(w.start(), w.count() + 1);
        if (n.count() > 100) return false;
        if (ref.compareAndSet(w, n)) return true;
    }
}
data class Window(val start: Long, val count: Int)
val ref = AtomicReference(Window(now(), 0))
fun allow(): Boolean {
    val now = System.nanoTime() / 1_000_000
    while (true) {
        val w = ref.get()
        val n = if (now - w.start >= 1000) Window(now, 1) else Window(w.start, w.count + 1)
        if (n.count > 100) return false
        if (ref.compareAndSet(w, n)) return true
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Multi-thread test with a fake clock and exact admitted count.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use currentTimeMillis for intervals (use monotonic nanoTime), and I would not call it correct without a test. A fixed window can still admit 2x at boundaries; sliding window solves that (verify requirements).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Millions of ops/s? -> Per-user sharding and LongAdder plus approximate limits.
  • Distributed? -> Redis counters with Lua or token bucket; out of LLD scope.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite limiter let a burst through during window flips and tripped a downstream rate limit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot find it.
  • Hire: states two atomics are not atomic as a pair.
  • Strong hire: single immutable state with CAS, monotonic clock, fixed-window caveat.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate's test for the parking lot passes locally and fails 1 in 20 on CI:

@Test void feeIsThreeHours() throws Exception {
    Ticket t = lot.park(CAR);
    Thread.sleep(3 * 60 * 60 * 1000);   // CI timeout after 10 min
    assertEquals(120, lot.unpark(t).rupees());
}
@Test void parksConcurrently() {
    new Thread(() -> lot.park(CAR)).start();
    new Thread(() -> lot.park(CAR)).start();
    assertEquals(2, lot.occupied());
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with both tests and how do you rewrite them?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Reduces the sleep to 100 ms or adds a longer sleep to the second test.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the lot take a Clock? Is the second test supposed to prove thread safety?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Mark the flaky test quarantined and fix it in the same PR.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) real sleeping in a time test; (b) no synchronization: the asserts may run before threads finish; (c) it does not test contention.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the test 200 times; look at the failure order.
  5. Root cause: Time and threads are not controlled by the test.
  6. Fix: Injected Clock for the fee; latches and a pool for concurrency.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
Clock c = new MutableClock(Instant.parse("2026-01-01T10:00:00Z"));
ParkingLot lot = new ParkingLot(pricing, c);
Ticket t = lot.park(CAR);
c.advance(Duration.ofHours(3));
assertEquals(120, lot.unpark(t).rupees());

@Test void neverOversells() throws Exception {
    Level level = new Level(10);
    ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
    AtomicInteger ok = new AtomicInteger();
    CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1), done = new CountDownLatch(100);
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) pool.submit(() -> {
        try { go.await(); if (level.park(CAR).isPresent()) ok.incrementAndGet(); }
        catch (InterruptedException ignored) {} finally { done.countDown(); }
    });
    go.countDown(); done.await();
    assertEquals(10, ok.get());
    pool.shutdown();
}
val clock = MutableClock(Instant.parse("2026-01-01T10:00:00Z"))
val lot = ParkingLot(pricing, clock)
val t = lot.park(CAR); clock.advance(Duration.ofHours(3))
assertEquals(120, lot.unpark(t).rupees)
  1. Prevention: No Thread.sleep in tests; run concurrency tests repeatedly; treat flakiness as a bug.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not mock everything; fakes for the clock and pricing are enough. A passing concurrency test is not proof; add lock-order review and, for deep checks, jcstress (verify fit).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Coroutines? -> runTest with virtual time.
  • Test passes by luck? -> Run in a loop (for example 1,000 iterations) and use more threads than cores.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite suite lost two engineer-days a month to flaky sleeps until a Clock was injected.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks the sleep.
  • Hire: Clock plus latch-based test.
  • Strong hire: exact assertions (10, not 11), repetition, and limits of testing concurrency.

questions.contextHtml:
A thumbnail service accepts 800 jobs/s and processes 300/s using Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8). After 20 minutes pods restart with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Heap histogram:

 num   #instances     #bytes  class name
   1:   2,400,000   1,150,000,000  com.acme.ThumbnailJob
   2:   2,400,000      230,400,000  java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue$Node

CPU is at 100% on 8 cores; GC time is rising.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it die and what is the correct design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can jobs be dropped or delayed? Is the producer HTTP (can return 429) or a queue? Are jobs idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load: return 429/503 for new jobs; scale workers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) unbounded queue absorbing the 500/s deficit: 500 x 1,200 s = 600,000 jobs after 20 minutes, and the histogram says 2.4 million; (b) memory leak in jobs (the jobs are the bulk, consistent with the queue); (c) GC tuning (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: jmap -histo, queue-size metric growth, and arrival-versus-service rate math.
  5. Root cause: newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue: no back-pressure.
  6. Fix: Build a bounded pool with a rejection policy.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
ExecutorService ex = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000), new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
val ex = ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0L, TimeUnit.SECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(1000), ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy())

For I/O-bound work size the pool as cores x (1 + wait/compute); Java 21 virtual threads help I/O-bound cases. 7. Prevention: Alert on queue depth and rejection count; load-test above capacity. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: CallerRunsPolicy slows producers (good back-pressure) but can block the request thread; a 429 is better for an HTTP front end. I would not raise the heap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Jobs must not be lost? -> Persist to a durable queue, not memory.
  • Which rejection policy? -> Abort with 429 to shed, caller-runs to throttle.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite service ran fine for months until one slow dependency doubled job time and the unbounded queue ate the heap.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more memory.
  • Hire: bounded queue and rejection policy with math.
  • Strong hire: back-pressure design, metrics, durable queue and pool sizing.

questions.promptHtml: Which Java habits make an LLD answer look senior? Pick the five you would never skip and justify them.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The small choices (money, time, nullability, immutability) predict code review quality.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Immutability by default (final, records, List.copyOf), constructor injection against interfaces, fail fast with Optional instead of null, money as BigDecimal or integer minor units and time via java.time with an injected Clock, and documented thread-safety. Also equals/hashCode together for map keys, and never swallowing InterruptedException.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Replacing double fee with long feePaise plus a Duration input avoids rounding bugs (0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3). SimpleDateFormat and Date are not thread-safe. Restore the interrupt flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public record Ticket(String id, int spotId, Instant entry) {
    public Ticket {
        Objects.requireNonNull(id); Objects.requireNonNull(entry);
        if (spotId < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("spotId");
    }
}
data class Ticket(val id: String, val spotId: Int, val entry: Instant) {
    init { require(spotId >= 0) { "spotId" } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mutable DTOs shared across threads.
  • Catching InterruptedException and ignoring it.
  • Using double for money, Date/Calendar.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a record? -> Immutable value with equals/hashCode/toString for free.
  2. Checked vs unchecked? -> Domain errors as small unchecked exceptions; checked where callers can recover.
  3. Optional as a field? -> Avoid; use it for return values.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: writes working code. Senior: shows the habits unprompted and explains each in a sentence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A double price calculation drifted by one paisa per thousand orders and failed reconciliation.

questions.contextHtml: You inherit a 600-line ParkingLot with 25 methods: spot search, fee calculation, ticket persistence to a file, SMS sending, and printing. A concurrency fix needs one lock, but unrelated features keep colliding in merges and the single lock blocks SMS sending and parking together. Tests need a real file and a real SMS stub.
questions.promptHtml: Show the new classes, the patterns you actually use, and the order of the refactor.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Introduces Factory, Observer and Singleton everywhere at once.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changes most often? Which parts need different locking? Are there tests to protect the behavior?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add characterization tests for park/unpark before touching code.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) responsibilities: allocation, pricing, persistence, notification; (b) the lock is too coarse because unrelated work shares it; (c) premature patterns would add noise.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group methods by data they use; count reasons to change.
  5. Root cause: One class with several reasons to change.
  6. Fix: Extract one role at a time, behind small interfaces:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class ParkingLot { /* orchestrates */ }
class SpotAllocator { Optional<Spot> allocate(VehicleType t) {...} }
interface PricingStrategy { Money fee(Duration d, VehicleType t); }
interface TicketRepository { void save(Ticket t); Optional<Ticket> find(String id); }
interface Notifier { void send(Ticket t); }
class ParkingLot(private val allocator: SpotAllocator, private val pricing: PricingStrategy,
                 private val tickets: TicketRepository, private val notifier: Notifier)

Order: pricing first (pure, easiest), then repository, then notifier, then allocator (carries the lock). Only pricing and notification vary by requirement; the rest stay plain classes. 7. Prevention: Class size and complexity checks in CI; a pattern needs a named second variant. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No big-bang rewrite; no pattern with a single implementation unless tests need it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lock scope after the split? -> Only the allocator's claim step; SMS runs outside any lock.
  • Is Singleton needed for the lot? -> No; the composition root creates one.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite 600-line manager became five 100-line classes; the review time per PR dropped and the SMS outage no longer blocked parking.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: patterns everywhere.
  • Hire: split by responsibility with interfaces where things vary.
  • Strong hire: characterization tests, ordered refactor, lock scope reasoning.

questions.contextHtml:
You review a candidate's wallet snippet. Production stakes: money, multiple threads.

public class Wallet {
    public double balance;
    public static Map<String, Wallet> all = new HashMap<>();
    public Wallet get(String id) { return all.get(id); }           // null when missing
    public void pay(double amt) {
        try { Thread.sleep(10); } catch (InterruptedException e) {}
        balance -= amt;
    }
    public String today() { return new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd").format(new Date()); }
}
questions.promptHtml: List the problems in priority order and show the corrected core.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only mentions double.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Wallet shared across threads? Can balance go negative? What currency and minor unit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) public mutable balance and race on -= (lost updates); (2) double for money; (3) static mutable HashMap (not thread-safe, global state); (4) null return for not found; (5) swallowed InterruptedException; (6) SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe and Date is legacy; (7) no validation (overdraft, negative amounts).
  4. How I'd verify each: A 16-thread test debiting 1 each 10,000 times: the result is not 0. Re-run under load for HashMap corruption.
  5. Root cause: Several violations of the immutability, encapsulation and concurrency rules.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
public final class Wallet {
    private final String id; private long balancePaise;           // guarded by this
    public Wallet(String id, long openingPaise) { this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id); this.balancePaise = openingPaise; }
    public synchronized void pay(long paise) {
        if (paise <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("paise");
        if (paise > balancePaise) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        balancePaise -= paise;
    }
    public synchronized long balance() { return balancePaise; }
}
class WalletRepository {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Wallet> byId = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    Optional<Wallet> find(String id) { return Optional.ofNullable(byId.get(id)); }
}
String today(Clock c) { return LocalDate.now(c).toString(); }
class Wallet(val id: String, opening: Long) {
    private var balance = opening
    @Synchronized fun pay(paise: Long) {
        require(paise > 0); check(paise <= balance) { "insufficient funds" }; balance -= paise
    }
    @Synchronized fun balance() = balance
}

If interrupted: Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and return, never swallow. 7. Prevention: Static analysis for public fields and double money; concurrency test. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep static state, and I would not add synchronized to every method without naming the guarded invariant.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Transfers between two wallets? -> Lock ordering by id.
  • BigDecimal vs paise? -> Both fine; paise as long is simple and fast; BigDecimal when fractional minor units exist.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite wallet used double, drifted over a month, and failed reconciliation by a few rupees.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only double.
  • Hire: race, money, static map, null and InterruptedException.
  • Strong hire: prioritised list, fixed core, tests and the transfer deadlock follow-up.
